Nice, I like the energy. So walk me through your background a bit—how'd you end up where you are now?

Sure. I'm finishing a communications degree, and I've been a marketing intern at a local coffee chain for the past year or so. What got me into it was seeing how a small change, like a better photo or a clearer message, could actually get customers to show up. So I started asking to take on projects, and that's pretty much how I ended up doing social, email, and events for the company. I like that it's hands-on and you can see whether something worked.
Got it. So you've got a pretty wide range of stuff under your belt there. Let me ask you about a time you failed at something.

Honestly, the closest thing was our store launch event. The speaker cancelled the day before, and I had a moment of panic because the whole night was built around that talk. I ended up booking a barista for a latte-art demo, and 214 people still came through the door on a $1,500 budget. What I took from it is to always have a backup plan for anything that depends on one person showing up.
That's helpful context. What would you have done differently if you could do it over?

I'd have lined up a backup speaker a couple weeks out, not the day before. I was so focused on getting the main speaker locked in that I didn't think about what happens if they drop out. Even a rough shortlist of two or three other people would have made that panic a lot smaller. The demo worked out, but I'd rather not have been scrambling at all.
Makes sense. Let's switch gears—why do you want this kind of role, like marketing or communications work?

I like that marketing is where creative ideas meet actual numbers. When I changed our Instagram from product photos to short customer videos, I could watch the engagement rate go from about 2.0% to 2.8% over three months, and that kind of feedback is what keeps me interested. I also like that communications lets me think about how people feel when they read something, not just whether they clicked. I want a job where I can keep testing ideas and seeing what actually moves people.
Got it. You mentioned growing Instagram engagement—was that the 40% you have on your resume, or something different?

Yes, that's the 40%. Our average engagement rate per post went from about 2.0% to 2.8% over three months, and that works out to roughly a 40% increase. I switched us from product photos to short customer videos, and my manager approved the plan before we started. I'd want to be clear that it was a team effort with my manager's sign-off, but the content direction was my call.
Thanks. When you say the content direction was your call, what exactly did you do—like, did you shoot the videos, write the captions, pick which ones to post?

Mostly I was the one planning and running it. I set up a simple schedule for the videos and decided which customer clips to pull from the ones we'd already gotten, because a lot of people had tagged us in their own stories. I wrote most of the captions and did the editing in a basic app to keep them short. I didn't do the filming myself in every case, since some of the clips came from customers, and I didn't shoot the in-store stuff that the baristas handled. So I'd say I owned the plan, the selection, and the copy, and I checked the numbers every couple of weeks to see what was working.
Got it. When you checked the numbers every couple of weeks, what were you actually looking at—like, which metrics mattered most to you?

Mainly engagement rate per post, which is likes, comments, and shares divided by reach. I kept an eye on that because it tells you how people respond to what you put out, not just how many people saw it. I also looked at which videos got saved or shared, since those usually meant people found them useful or funny enough to pass along. Follower count moved slowly, so I didn't lean on it much. If a video was getting a lot of views but few comments, I'd look at whether the opening was too slow.
Got it. Let's switch to the store launch event you planned for 200 guests. Walk me through what that involved.

Sure. We were launching a new store, and I planned the whole evening for about 200 guests. I handled the invitations, the timing, and the flow of the night, and I worked within a $1,500 budget. The main draw was a speaker, and then they cancelled the day before, so I had to pivot fast. I booked a barista for a latte-art demo, which ended up being a crowd favorite. Good question. I wrote the invitations and sent them out through our email list and Instagram, and I set the run-of-show, meaning when the doors opened, when the speaker was supposed to start, and when the demo would go. My manager signed off on the budget and the venue. The store manager and baristas handled setup, the drinks, and the day-of coverage, and a friend on the marketing side helped me print signage. When the speaker dropped out, I made the call on the demo and then ran it past my manager, who said yes.
Got it. So when the speaker dropped out, how much notice did you get, and what exactly did you do to pivot to the demo instead?

The speaker cancelled the day before, so I had roughly a day's notice. I called the barista lead that afternoon to see who had done latte art before and could put together a short demo. We picked one of our baristas who was really good at it, and I worked out a 20 to 30 minute slot with her so it fit into the flow of the night. I also updated the run-of-show and let the store manager know what changed, and then I let my manager know and got a yes. Honestly, it was a lot of scrambling for one evening, but the demo ended up being one of the things people talked about.

We were getting an open rate of about 18%, and I wanted to get that up. The biggest change was rewriting the subject lines so they were specific and short, instead of vague announcements. I don't have the exact before-and-after wording in front of me, so I don't want to make one up. But the pattern was pretty consistent. An old one might have been something like "Updates from our store," which tells you nothing. I'd rewrite it to name the actual thing in the email, like a specific drink or a date, and keep it short enough to read on a phone. I also tested a couple of versions before settling on the style we kept.
That makes sense. Out of curiosity, how'd you test those versions—did you send them to a small group first, or another way?
Actually, let's leave it there, since we're just about out of time. Before we wrap up, what questions do you have for me?
Sure, just one. What does the first few months look like for someone in this role, and what would you most want them to get good at?

Good question. The first few months are really about learning the team, the product, and how we work—shadowing, asking questions, taking on smaller projects to build momentum. What matters most is that you get comfortable making decisions with incomplete information and owning the outcomes, whatever they are. Thanks again for your time, and have a great day.
